Metadata

Abstract:

In this article, we propose an approximate optimal control strategy for a class of nonlinear multiagent system pursuit–evasion games. Herein, multiple pursuers aim to capture multiple evaders trying to evade capture. Under the competitive framework, agents not only pursue their individual goals but also consider coordination with their teammates to achieve collective objectives. However, maintaining cohesion with teammates in existing distributed control methods has always been a challenge. To enhance team coordination, we employ a graph-theoretic approach to represent the relationships between agents. Based on this, we design a dynamic target graph algorithm to enhance the coordination among pursuers. The approximate optimal strategies for each agent are solved by utilizing the Hamilton–Jacobi–Isaacs equations of the system. As solving these equations becomes computationally intensive in multiagent scenarios, we propose a value-based single network adaptive critic network architecture. In addition, we consider scenarios where the numbers of agents on both sides are inconsistent and address the phenomenon of input saturation. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions to prove the system's stability. Finally, simulations conducted in two representative scenarios, multiple-pursuer-one-evader and multiple-pursuer-multiple-evader, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm.

Contents
SECTION I.

Introduction

In The past decades, the pursuit–evasion (PE) game has emerged as a prominent and intriguing research topic, drawing significant attention. The pursuers and evaders, which participate in the PE game and possess capabilities in perception, communication, and action, are collectively referred to as agents. The multiagent system pursuit–evasion (MPE) game is a complex extension of the PE game, involving multiple agents. Specifically, the objective of the pursuers is to minimize the distance to their targeted evaders and achieve interception while the evaders aim to evade or delay interception. Unlike evaders who engage in passive avoidance, pursuers possess the flexibility to select different targets as their objectives. The MPE game initially arose in natural animal hunting scenarios and have since been further developed with the concepts of game theory. The MPE game finds wide engineering applications in areas, such as autonomous aerial vehicles, satellites, mobile robot systems, vicinagearth security, and sports/game strategy [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6].

The single-pursuer single-evader game was initially studied based on the differential game framework involving two players, which is a zero-sum game. In most PE games, the pursuer's objective of minimizing the distance to the evader is represented through value functions. These individual performance indices are then used to define equilibrium points of the game [7]. By differentiating the value functions, Jang and Tomlin [8] achieved PE between aircraft. Jagat and Sinclair [9] based on the state-dependent Riccati equation methods designed a nonlinear control approach for the spacecraft PE game. Later, the PE game was extended to the multiple-pursuer single-evader scenario [10], where pursuers can form certain formations through formation control. When the PE game is extended to the multiple-pursuer multiple-evader scenario, it is referred to as MPE [11]. In [12], different types of pursuers are designed, and the PE relationships are studied based on an N-player nonzero-sum game framework.

In MPE scenarios with multiple agents, the relationships among them become more complex [13], [14], [15]. To handle these relationships, graph-theoretic approaches have been utilized, as demonstrated in [16] and [17] and applied to PE games with linear dynamics in [11]. In [18], the pursuer, acting as a child node, is paired with the evader acting as a parent node; this topological relationship is fixed. Consequently, when assistance is required from another child node's pursuers, the inability to change the topological relationship leads to an inability to leverage team effectiveness. In [17], the MPE game is decomposed into several MPE game subsystems. While the behavior within each subsystem does not influence the stability of the overall environment, there is an inherent lack of collaborative interaction between the subsystems themselves. These methods design value functions that take into account the state difference with respect to the goal or neighboring nodes. Although each distributed strategy is goal-oriented, agents within the same team lack communication and collaboration. Therefore, achieving coordinated control with team collaboration remains a challenge in many distributed control algorithms [19], [20]. Consequently, the complex interactions among multiple agents to enhance team cohesion merit in-depth research [21]. Consensus, which is extensively studied for multiagent system control using graph theory [22], is often achieved in the context of formation control by defining desired displacements [23]. In this work, while enhancing cohesion through target switching, the role of desired displacements is also considered.

In practical applications, several MPE game processes often involve inherent nonlinearities [9], [24]. Consequently, solving the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Isaacs (HJI) equations becomes necessary, for which analytical solutions are not readily available [25], [26]. To address this issue, various adaptive dynamic programming algorithms have been proposed [27], [28], [29], [30]. In addition, based on the principle of optimality, reinforcement learning algorithms employing the actor–critic (AC) architecture have been widely utilized for learning optimal policies online in MPE problems [29], [30]. However, in the context of multiagent systems, each agent is equipped with its own actor and critic networks [1]. The existence of multiple networks, while necessary for decentralized decision-making, inadvertently increases the computational burden [31]. To enhance computational efficiency, a single network adaptive critic (SNAC) structure has been proposed for solving control-constrained optimal control problems [32], which eliminates the need for an action network. This structure was later applied to single-pursuer single-evader games within the framework of fault-tolerant control [33]. Literature surveys reveal that existing studies have implemented the SNAC structure in the context of single-agent PE games and multiagent adversarial problems [33], [34]. However, no studies have been found to explore the potential application of this approach within MPE systems. Therefore, one of the objectives of this article is to explore the potential of this structure in the MPE system.

Another aspect worth mentioning is that, in engineering applications, the output amplitudes of actuators often exhibit saturated nonlinearities due to physical limitations [35]. Therefore, many studies also take into account the design of controllers considering the actuator saturation phenomenon [36], [37]. Ignoring the actuator saturation phenomenon not only increases the risk of performance degradation and instability in controlled systems but also results in a partial detachment of research from practicality. Furthermore, the stability and reliability of the systems are of utmost importance. Currently, mainstream approximate optimal control methods construct Lyapunov functions to prove the uniformly boundedness of nonlinear closed-loop systems. The stability analysis of multiagent systems based on graph-theoretic approaches is investigated in [38] and [34].

According to the aforementioned discussion, conventional MPE games present some interesting challenges in designing coordinated capture strategies among all pursuers. In this article, our objective is to design an algorithm that combines reinforcement learning and dynamic target graphs to approximate optimal control strategies for MPE games under actuator saturation conditions. The contributions of this article are summarized as follows.

  1. A graph-theoretic approach is designed to represent the relationships among the agents, and based on this, a dynamic target graph algorithm is employed to enhance the coordination among the agents. Unlike the fixed communication graph in [17], [18], and [39], the weighted adjacency matrix of our graph is entirely dynamic, further improving the team cohesion among pursuers compared to [26].

  2. In contrast to existing results [12], [26], which solved MPE games under linear systems, our work considers the nonlinear dynamic of the system and actuator constraints. Moreover, unlike [33], our method can obtain solutions for various scenarios with different numbers of pursuers and evaders by solving the HJI equation, which implies that our algorithm faces a more complex environment.

  3. In the proposed method, we utilize the value-based single network adaptive critic (V-SNAC) network structure, which reduces the computational burden compared to the AC network structure [39], [40]. We validate the effectiveness of our algorithm in two typical scenarios: multiple-pursuer-single-evader and multiple-pursuer-multiple-evader. In addition, a comparison of the computational burden with the AC structure [39] has been implemented, and the results indicate that the V-SNAC structure can reduce computational time by approximately 31%.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II provides the preliminaries of the MPE problem, including the graph model and state equations. The solution strategies for the MPE game are proposed in Section III. The simulations and experiments for the two scenarios are presented in Section IV. Finally, Section V concludes this article.

SECTION II.

Preliminaries

A. Graph Theory

Consider an MPE scenario with Np pursuers and Ne evaders, where the entire system consists of Np+Ne agents. Define the graph Gp=(Vp,Ep) to represent the communication topology of Np pursuers. Set of nodes Vp={vp1,…,vpNp} and set of edges Ep⊆Vp×Vp. If and only pursuer m has access to the information of pursuer n, and we say agent n is a neighbor of agent m, i.e., (vpm,vpn)∈Ep. Let am,n be the communication weight of the graph Gp, with am,n=1 if (vpm,vpn)∈Ep and am,n=0 otherwise. Let Ap=[am,n]∈RNp×Np be the weighted adjacency matrix where am,m=0. Define the in-degree of pursuer m as dpm=∑Npn=1am,n and the in-degree matrix of the graph Dp=diag{dpm}. Then, the Laplacian matrix can be defined as Lp=Dp−Ap. Similarly, the graph Ge=(Ve,Ee) represents the interaction topology among Ne evaders with the nodes Ve={ve1,…,veNe}. The edge weights bm,n with bm,n=1 if (vem,ven)∈Ee and bm,n=0 otherwise. The in-degree of evader m as dem=∑Nen=1bm,n and the in-degree matrix of the graph De=diag{dem}. Defined the matrix Ae=[bm,n] as Le=De−Ae.

Define the bipartite graph G=(V,E) represent the target topology among pursuers and evaders. Specifically, for m∈Vp and n∈Ve, the edge weight cm,n=1 if pursuer m targets evader n and cm,n=0 otherwise. Similarly, en,m=1 if evader n targets pursuer m for evasion and en,m=0 otherwise. The in-degree of pursuer m in graph G is defined as dpem=∑Nen=1cm,n, and the in-degree of evader n is depn=∑Npm=1en,m. Define the pursuer-partition matrices Dpe=diag{dpem} and Ape=[cm,n], and the evader-partition matrices Dep=diag{depm} and Aep=[en,m].

Assumption 1:

For the MPE game problem in this article, it is assumed that agents on the same team can communicate and exchange information with each other. Each pursuer has access to the state information of their targeted evader, and conversely, each evader can obtain information about the pursuers who are targeting them as their objectives. Graphs Gp and Ge are connected graphs.

B. Problem Formulation

Consider a system comprising Np pursuers, each characterized by the following dynamics:

x˙pj=f(xpj)+g(xpj)upj(1)
View Source \begin{align*} \dot{x}_{j}^{p}=f\left({x}_{j}^{p}\right)+g\left({x}_{j}^{p}\right) u_{j}^{p} \tag{1} \end{align*} where j=1,…,Np, xpj∈Rn, is the system state of the jth pursuer, upj∈Rm denotes the control input of the jth pursuer.

Consider also a system with Ne evaders, each described by

x˙ei=f(xei)+g(xei)uei(2)
View Source \begin{align*} \dot{x}_{i}^{e}=f\left({x}_{i}^{e}\right)+g\left({x}_{i}^{e}\right) u_{i}^{e} \tag{2} \end{align*} where i=1,…,Ne, xei∈Rn, is the system state of the ith evader, uei∈Rm denotes the control input of the ith evader. upj and uei are both subjected to saturation constraint u¯p and u¯e, respectively, i.e., |upj|≤u¯p and |uei|≤u¯e. u¯p and u¯e are positive constant. f(⋅)∈Rn is the continuous nonlinear function and g(⋅)∈Rn×m is the continuous control gain function. In this article, we assumed that f(⋅),g(⋅) are Lipchitz functions on a compact set Ω1.

For each evader, define the state error variable between the pursuers and their target evader i as

x~pei=∑j=1Np(cj,i(xpj−xei+rpej,i))(3)
View Source \begin{align*} \tilde{x}_{i}^{\text{pe}} =\sum _{j=1}^{N_{p}}\left(c_{j,i}(x_{j}^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}})\right) \tag{3} \end{align*} where rpej,i is the expected displacement between the pursuer j and the evader i, and it can be a zero vector if necessary.

Using (1) and (2), it can be inferred that

x~˙pei=∑j=1Np(cj,i(f(xpj)−f(xei)+g(xpj)upj−g(xei)uei)).(4)
View Source \begin{align*} \dot{\tilde{x}}_{i}^{\text{pe}} =\sum _{j=1}^{N_{p}}\left(c_{j,i}(f\left({x}_{j}^{p}\right)-f\left({x}_{i}^{e}\right)+g\left({x}_{j}^{p}\right) u_{j}^{p}-g\left({x}_{i}^{e}\right) u_{i}^{e})\right) . \tag{4} \end{align*}

Remark 1:

In the MPE game framework considered in this article, we assume that the number of pursuers is greater than or equal to the number of evaders, i.e., Np≥Ne. If the number of evaders is greater, there will inevitably be some evaders escaping without facing any challenge, which is not within the scope of our analysis. Conversely, if the number of pursuers is greater, there can be cases where several pursuers simultaneously chase a single evader. The pursuers may aim to intercept the target evader by achieving surrounding formation control. The target allocation method, which will be discussed later in this article, contributes to better team cohesion among pursuers.

When considering the PE game involving multiple pursuers and evaders, the augmented system states are defined as follows:

Xp=⎡⎣⎢⎢⎢⎢xp1xp2⋯xpNp⎤⎦⎥⎥⎥⎥,Xe=⎡⎣⎢⎢⎢⎢xe1xe2⋯xeNe⎤⎦⎥⎥⎥⎥(5)
View Source \begin{align*} X^{p}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{p} \\ x_{2}^{p} \\ \cdots \\ x_{N_{p}}^{p} \end{bmatrix},\; X^{e}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{e} \\ x_{2}^{e} \\ \cdots \\ x_{N_{e}}^{e} \end{bmatrix}\; \tag{5} \end{align*} then the multiagent PE system based on (1) and (2) can be described as
X˙p=X˙e=F(Xp)+∑j=1NpGj(Xp)upjF(Xe)+∑i=1NeGi(Xe)uei(6)
View Source \begin{align*} \dot{X}^{p} =& F\left({X}^{p}\right)+\sum _{j = 1}^{N_{p}} G_{j}\left({X}^{p}\right) u_{j}^{p} \\ \dot{X}^{e} =& F\left({X}^{e}\right)+\sum _{i =1}^{N_{e}} G_{i}\left({X}^{e}\right) u_{i}^{e} \tag{6} \end{align*} where F(Xp)=[fT(xp1),…,fT(xpNp)]T, Gj(Xp)=[B1,…,Bj,…,BNp]T⊗[gT(xp1),…,gT(xpNp)]T with Bm=0n for m=1,…,Np, m≠j and Bm=In if m=j. In which ⊗ stands for Kronecker product. Similarly, F(Xe)=[fT(xe1),…,fT(xeNe)]T and Gi(Xe)=[D1,…,Di,…,DNe]T⊗[gT(xe1),…,gT(xeNe)]T with Dm=0n for m=1,…,Ne, m≠i and Dm=In if m=i.

In the following, for simplicity, we will write {fpj,fei} and {gpj,gei} to replace {f(xpj),f(xei)} and {g(xpj),g(xei)}, respectively.

SECTION III.

Objective Design and Solutions

A. Target Allocation and Objective Design

Define γj,i>0 as the weighted 2-norm of the state difference between a specific pursuer j and another evader i, given by γj,i=∥ν⊙(xpj−xei+rpej,i)∥, where ν∈Rn is the element weight and ⊙ stands for Hadamard product. Both velocity and position information are contained in the state. If there exists another pair of pursuer j′ and its target evader i′, where cj′,i=0 or cj,i′=0, it implies that pursuer j′ and evader i, as well as pursuer j and evader i′, do not form a target relationship. However, by exchanging their respective evader targets i and i′, pursuers j and j′ can achieve their objectives more easily. Consequently, the current weighted adjacency matrices Ape and Aep will be adjusted according to Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1: Dynamic Target Graph Algorithm.

Input: System states of pursuers {xpj} and evaders {xei}.

Specify the swap threshold ϱ≥0

Calculate the distance γj,i between all pursuers and evaders.

For evader ei,i≤Ne and pursuers pj,j≤Np

If (γj,i+γj′,i′)−(γj′,i+γj,i′)>ϱ

Swap their edge weights that exchanging cj,i with cj′,i and cj,i′ with cj′,i′. Update ej,i accordingly.

until comparison of other distances γ is completed.

Update the weighted adjacency matrix Ape and Aep.

Output: {Ape,Aep}.

Remark 2:

The swap threshold ϱ is crucial for ensuring significant benefits from target switches by pursuers. Increasing ϱ raises the switching barrier, potentially reducing the frequency or possibility of switches. Decreasing ϱ makes switching easier and more frequent, but excessive switching for trivial gains is impractical in engineering. The simulation section will carefully determine an appropriate ϱ value.

In order to quantify and measure the overall team cohesion of the pursuers, we define the team state error of pursuers with target topology obtained by Algorithm 1 as

ETeam=∑i=1Ne∑j=1Np(cj,i∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei+rpej,i)∥∥).(7)
View Source \begin{align*} E_{\text{Team}}=\sum _{i=1}^{N_{e}}\sum _{j=1}^{N_{p}}\left(c_{j,i} \left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \right). \tag{7} \end{align*} The team state error can reflect the overall state error within the team rather than the error of individual agents. The smaller the team state error, the stronger the team cohesion is considered to be. Subsequently, we analyze the enhancement of cohesion from a mathematical perspective.

Theorem 1:

Consider two arbitrary scenarios A and B, each characterized by identical MPE game dynamics described in (6). Scenario A uses algorithm 2 to dynamically allocate targets, and scenario B uses the initial fixed target topology. The team state errors of scenarios A and B are defined as ETeam and Eoteam, respectively. Then, Eteam≤Eoteam holds.

Proof:

Based on Algorithm 1, If the condition (γj,i+γj′,i′)−(γj′,i+γj,i′)>ϱ is not triggered, due to the same initial target topology, the two methods have the same adjacency matrix from beginning to end, and subsequently ETeam=EOTeam.

If at a certain time step t, two pursuers exchange their target evaders, it can be described as cj,i=0,cj′,i′=0,cj′,i=1,cj,i′=1 to the state where cj,i=1,cj′,i′=1,cj′,i=0,cj,i′=0. Let x~uc and x~ouc be defined as the sums of the unchanged target topology part of the state errors for ETeam and EOTeam, respectively. Then, ETeam and EOTeam can be reformulated as

ETeam=EOTeam=x~uc+∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei+rpej,i)∥∥+∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥x~ouc+∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei+rpej,i)∥∥+∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥.(8)
View Source \begin{align*} E_{\text{Team}}=& \tilde{x}_{\text{uc}} + \left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ & +\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ E_{\text{Team}}^{O}=& \tilde{x}_{\text{uc}}^{o} + \left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ & +\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert. \tag{8} \end{align*} Based on (8), we calculate the difference between the team error states ETeam and EOTeam at time step t, i.e.,
ETeam−EOTeam=∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei+rpej,i)∥∥+∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥−∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei+rpej,i)∥∥−∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥.(9)
View Source \begin{align*} &E_{\text{Team}}-E_{\text{Team}}^{O} =\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ &\quad +\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert -\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ &\quad -\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert. \tag{9} \end{align*} Since
(γj,i+γj′,i′)−(γj′,i+γj,i′)=∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei+rpej,i)∥∥+∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥−∥∥ν⊙(xpj′−xei+rpej,i)∥∥−∥∥ν⊙(xpj−xei′+rpej,i)∥∥>ϱ.(10)
View Source \begin{align*} &(\gamma _{j,i}+\gamma _{j^\prime,i^\prime })-(\gamma _{j^\prime,i}+\gamma _{j,i^\prime }) \\ &=\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert + \left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert \\ &-\left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j^\prime }^{p}-x_{i}^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert - \left\Vert \nu \odot (x_{j}^{p}-x_{i^\prime }^{e}+r_{j,i}^{\text{pe}}) \right\Vert >\varrho. \tag{10} \end{align*} It can be deduced that
ETeam−EOTeam≤−ϱ<0.(11)
View Source \begin{align*} E_{\text{Team}}-E_{\text{Team}}^{O}\leq -\varrho < 0. \tag{11} \end{align*} Since the previous values of cj,i,cj′,i′,cj′,i, and cj,i′ are actually arbitrarily chosen, therefore, by the same token, any subsequent exchange will satisfy ETeam≤EOTeam, thereby mathematically demonstrating the enhancement of cohesion.■

Based on Algorithm 1 and Theorem 1, dynamic target assignment prioritizes team cohesion over individual optimization by reducing the pursuer team's overall cost. To quantify the outcome of the MPE game, for each target evader, the cost function Ji is defined as

Ji(x0,upj,uei)=∫∞0(Pi(x)+U(upj)−W(uei))dt(12)
View Source \begin{align*} J_{i}\left(x_{0}, u_{j}^{p}, u_{i}^{e}\right)=\int _{0}^{\infty }\left(P_{i}(x)+U(u_{j}^{p})-W(u_{i}^{e})\right) \mathrm{d}t \tag{12} \end{align*} where Pi(x) is defined as
Pi(x)=(x~pei)TQx~pei(13)
View Source \begin{align*} P_{i}(x)=(\tilde{x}_{i}^{\text{pe}})^{T}Q\tilde{x}_{i}^{\text{pe}} \tag{13} \end{align*} and [32]
⎧⎩⎨⎪⎪U(upj)=∑Npj=1(2ci,j∫upj0(u¯ptanh−1τu¯p)TR1dτ)W(uei)=2depi∫uei0(u¯etanh−1τu¯e)TR2dτ(14)
View Source \begin{align*} \left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll} U(u_{j}^{p})= \sum _{j=1}^{N_{p}} \left(2c_{i,j}\int _{0}^{u_{j}^{p}}(\bar{u}_{p}\tanh ^{-1}\frac{\tau }{\bar{u}_{p}})^{T}R_{1}\mathrm{d}\tau \right)\\ W(u_{i}^{e})=2d_{i}^{\text{ep}}\int _{0}^{u_{i}^{e}}(\bar{u}_{e}\tanh ^{-1}\frac{\tau }{\bar{u}_{e}})^{T}R_{2}\mathrm{d}\tau \end{array}\right. \tag{14} \end{align*} with positive-definite matrices Q∈Rn×n and R1,R2∈Rm×m. Taking into the factor of actuator saturation, nonquadratic functions U(⋅):Rm→R and W(⋅):Rm→R are designed to constrain the control input upj and uei within u¯p and u¯e, respectively.

Definition 1:

A series of control policies upj={up1,…,upNp} and uei={ue1,…,ueNe} are defined to be admissible with respect to (12) over Ω2∈Rn, if {upj,uei} are continuous over Ω2 and the control pair {upj,uei} stabilizes (6) over Ω2, and (12) is finite.

According to the control objective, pursuers aim to minimize function Ji(x0,upj,uei), while the evaders aim to maximize the performance function Ji(x0,upj,uei) by designing their respective control input upj and uei. Upon achieving equilibrium conditions in the PE game, as per the Nash–Pontryagin minimax principle, this state is referred to as a saddle point equilibrium (SPE). There is no motivation for any agents to deviate from the equilibrium. In the following, the definition of SPE is presented [41].

Definition 2:

Consider the MPE game in this article. Every pair of control strategies (up∗j,ue∗i) is said to be the SPE solution if

Ji(x(0),up∗j,uei)≤Ji(x(0),up∗j,ue∗i)≤Ji(x(0),upj,ue∗i).(15)
View Source \begin{align*} J_{i}\left(x(0),u_{j}^{p*},u_{i}^{e}\right)\leq J_{i}\left(x(0),u_{j}^{p*},u_{i}^{e*}\right)\leq J_{i}\left(x(0),u_{j}^{p},u_{i}^{e*}\right). \tag{15} \end{align*}

Define the value functions associated with admissible control policy as

Vi(x)=∫∞t(Pi(x)+U(upj)−W(uei))dτ.(16)
View Source \begin{align*} V_{i}(x)=\int _{t}^{\infty }\left(P_{i}(x)+U(u_{j}^{p})-W(u_{i}^{e})\right) \mathrm{d}\tau. \tag{16} \end{align*} The optimal value functions V∗i(x) is defined as
V∗i(x)=min{upj,uei}∈Ω2(∫∞t(Pi(x)+U(upj)−W(uei))dτ).(17)

B. PI Algorithm for MPE Game

In this section, the HJI equation will be introduced, which is used to derive the optimal control strategy {up∗j,ue∗i} and the value functions V∗i(x). The concept of admissible control is defined in Definition 1. Then, the subsequent best-response HJI equation, serving as the Bellman equation for the system, is defined as

H∗i=Pi(x)+U(up∗j)−W(ue∗i)+∇TVi(x)(∑j=1Np(cj,i(Fj,i(x)+gpjup∗j−geiue∗i)))=0(21)

Algorithm 2: Policy Iteration Algorithm.

Input: System initial states {xpj,xei} and their corresponding initial admissible control policy {μpj,0,μei,0}.

Initialize the error threshold ξ. Set V0i=0, and let s=0.

repeat

Based on the control pair {μpj,s,μei,s}, solve the equation (26) to obtain the value functions Vs+1i

Update the control policy μpj,s and μei,s simultaneously by

μpj,s=μei,s=−u¯ptanh(12u¯pR−11(gpj)T∇Vs+1i(x))−u¯etanh(12u¯eR−12(gei)T∇Vs+1i(x)).(25)

Update the weighted adjacency matrix Ape and Aep simultaneously by using Algorithm 1.

Set s=s+1.

until |Vsi−Vs−1i|<ξ

Output: {μpj,s,μei,s}.

Remark 3:

In this article, the control strategy for each agent is distributed. However, in Algorithm 2, each agent's solution of the HJI equation requires knowledge of the dynamics of the associated agent, which is implied in ∇Vs+1i(x) in (25). This restricts the application of the results. Therefore, in the next section, we will improve Algorithm 2 to achieve distributed control.

Thus, the approximate HJI function can be simplified as

H∗i=Pi(x)+∑j=1Np(cj,iu¯2pR¯1ln(1⃗ −tanh2(ρp(V∗i))))−depiu¯2eR¯2ln(1⃗ −tanh2(ρe(V∗i)))+∇TV∗i(x)(∑j=1Np(cj,iFj,i(x)))=0.(26)

Then, to solve the HJI approximate equations, the on-policy PI algorithm is put forward in Algorithm 2.

In the realm of PE games involving nonlinear systems, Yuan et al. [33] conducted pertinent research. However, the property for MPE games has not been sufficiently explored. In the following, we will demonstrate the convergence of the on-policy PI algorithm for MPE games. The analysis is based on the work of [43].

Theorem 2:

Consider the system of MPE game described by (6) with admissible control pair {μpj,s,μei,s} obtained by (25) in Algorithm 2. If the system model parameters F(Xp), F(Xe) and Gi(Xp), Gi(Xe) are known, then the iterative value functions will converge to V∗i(x), as s→∞.

Hi(Vi(x))≜Pi(x)+∑j=1Np(cj,iu¯2pR¯1ln(1⃗ −tanh2(ρp(Vi))))−depiu¯2eR¯2ln(1⃗ −tanh2(ρe(Vi)))+∇TVi(x)(∑j=1Np(cj,iFj,i(x)))=0.(27)

Definition 3:

Let H:U⊆X→Y be a given map with X and Y Banach spaces, where U(V) denotes a neighborhood of V. The map H is Gâteaux differentiable at V if and only there exists a bounded linear operator L:X→Y such that [25], [45]

To compute the Fréchet derivative, we introduce the following Lemma 1.

Lemma 1 (see [46]):

If the Gâteaux derivative L exists in some neighborhood of V and L is continuous at V, then L=H′(V) is also an Fréchet derivative at V.

Then, we compute the Fréchet derivative in the following Lemma 2 by (29).

C. Off-Policy RL Algorithm Design

In this section, an off-policy RL algorithm based on the foundation of Algorithm 2 is proposed. Note that Algorithm 2 requires the knowledge of value functions Vi(x) to solve the approximate HJI equation. Thus, we leverage the approximating characteristics of neural networks to address this issue. In the case of multiple agents, the application of multiple networks introduces computational burden. Therefore, we adopt the V-SNAC structure. In this structure, for each evader, only one critic network is utilized to captures the mapping between states and the value functions Vi(x). In MPE game, all the agents will continuously and simultaneously update the network weights. Therefore, the value functions Vi(x) can be approximated by critic network as

V∗i(x)=WTiψi(x)+δi(x)(37)

And the value solution V∗i(x) approximated by critic network at step s are reconstructed as

V^si(x)=W^Ti,sψi(x)(38)

Then, the off-policy RL algorithm for MPE game is summarized as Algorithm 3.

Algorithm 3: Off-Policy RL Algorithm.

Input: System states {xpj,xei} and their corresponding initial admissible control policy {μpj,0,μei,0}.

Initialize the error threshold ϵ, select an initial estimated weight vector W^i,0. Set s=0.

repeat

Based on the control pair {μpj,s,μei,s}, solve (41) by using (46) to update the W^i,s.

Update the control policy μpj,s and μei,s simultaneously by

⎧⎩⎨⎪⎪μpj,s=−u¯ptanh(12u¯pR−11(gpj)T∇ψTi(x)W^i,s)μei,s=−u¯etanh(12u¯eR−12(gei)T∇ψTi(x)W^i,s).
View Source \begin{align*} \left\lbrace \begin{array}{ll}\mu _{j,s}^{p}=-\bar{u}_{p}\tanh \left(\frac{1}{2\bar{u}_{p}}R_{1}^{-1}(g_{j}^{p})^{T} \nabla \psi _{i} ^{T}(x)\hat{W}_{i,s}\right)\\ \mu _{i,s}^{e}=-\bar{u}_{e}\tanh \left(\frac{1}{2\bar{u}_{e}}R_{2}^{-1}(g_{i}^{e})^{T}\nabla \psi _{i} ^{T}(x)\hat{W}_{i,s}\right). \end{array}\right. \end{align*}

Update the weighted adjacency matrix Ape and Aep simultaneously by using Algorithm 1.

Set s=s+1.

until |W^i,s−W^i,s−1|<ϵ.

Output: {μpj,s,μei,s}.

Remark 4:

The Algorithm 3 mainly includes the policy evaluation stage and policy improvement stage. To begin with, the correlative system data are collected. Then, the gradient descent algorithm is used to update the corresponding estimated weight. At last, the optimal control policies for MPE game with constrained inputs are iterated out. After the update of the weight adjacency matrix in each iteration, the corresponding edge weights in (41) will also be updated accordingly. Furthermore, to minimize the target function Esi, the estimated weight W^i,s can be calculated using (46). For the MPE game, we can calculate the optimal control policies with only one formula to replace (26) and (25) in Algorithm 2.

In Theorems 2 and 3, the convergent property of Algorithm 2 is proved. In the following, the convergence of the weights of critic network based on off-policy RL algorithm is analyzed. And thus, we can infer that V^si(x)→Vsi(x).■

Remark 5:

It has been proven that the magnitude of the weight estimation error is bounded within a finite region. To further ensure the convergence of the weight estimation error W~i,s, such that the residual error magnitude remains within an acceptable range, the persistency of excitation assumption is provided [49], i.e., Assumption 3. For the implementation process, the persistency of excitation condition is satisfied by utilizing exploration noises added to the given control inputs. These noises introduce variability into the inputs, thereby maintaining the necessary level of excitation to ensure the desired convergence properties.

SECTION IV.

Simulation

In this section, an MPE example based on the nonlinear aircraft system is presented to validate the effectiveness of the proposed off-policy RL control algorithm. Here, we present two simulation scenarios: multiple-pursuer-one-evader and multiple-pursuer-multiple-evader. In addition, we analyze the impact of saturation constraints, conduct comparative experiments on cohesion, and assess computational burden.

A. Nonlinear Aircraft Model

Consider an MPE game with agents described by (6) in R3. Letting system states (1) and (2) are both composed of xai, xbi, hi, v˘a,i, v˘b,i, and vh,i. Control input both composed of uai, ubi, uhi. According to [50], the dynamics of a simplified nonlinear aircraft model is designed as

B. Scenario 1: Multiple-Pursuer-One-Evader

Consider an MPE game involving three pursuers and one evader in R3, where the dynamics of each agent are governed by system (53) and (54). This serves as a representative example of a more pursuers than evaders scenario. In the example, the initial conditions are xp1=[600,−1900,300,78,2,18]T, xp2=[1200,500,2200,2,20,15]T, xp3=[200,600,800,5,10,125]T, xe1=[500,1500,200;50;80;10]. Select Q=I, R1=R2=I, u¯p=35, u¯e=15, αi=0.01 and the input constraint u¯p=25, u¯e=15. The expected displacement is given by rpe1,1=[50,10,0,0,0,0], rpe2,1=[10,50,0,0,0,0], and rpe3,1=[−10,0,−50,0,0,0]. Those varying expected displacements aid the pursuers in effectively surrounding the evader. The activation functions ψi(⋅) are selected as sigmoid functions. Then, the capture results of the three-pursuer-one-evader trajectory are shown in Fig. 1. From Fig. 1, it is obvious that at the beginning of the simulation, there is a considerable distance between the pursuers and the evader. After a brief adjustment, the distances between the three pursuers and the evader quickly reduce to a very small value and are maintained thereafter. And the state error between the pursuers and the evader is presented in Fig. 2. Fig. 3 shows the control inputs upi,s and uei,s of the pursuers and the evader, respectively. From Fig. 3, it can be observed that the constraints on saturated inputs are effectively implemented.

As a comparative experiment, under the same conditions, we have implemented MPE experiments using the target topology in [26]. The corresponding trajectory and state error are shown in Figs. 8 and 9, respectively. In existing works [17], [18], [39] on the MPE problem with fixed topologies, different control strategies are employed, but all use graphs to model agent interactions. According to Theorem 1, the dynamic target graph method introduced here can further reduce the team state error and boost team cohesion in these fixed-topology approaches. The team state error calculated by (7) is utilized to compare team cohesion. Smaller team state error indicating stronger cohesion among the pursuer team. It can be observed from Fig. 10 that our method exhibits faster reduction in team state error and demonstrates better team cohesion.

The convergence curves of W^i,s are displayed in Fig. 11. Thus, the approximate value functions converge to the optimal ones within a small bound. To elaborate, the weight vector W^1,s converges to [0.1468,0.1883,0.1986,0.3042,0.2033,0.4002]T, the weight vector W^2,s converges to [0.1943,0.1545,0.1995,0.3012,0.3051,0.3001]T, and the weight vector W^3,s converges to [0.1372,0.1930,0.1985,0.3094,0.1978,0.4003]T at the end of the simulation. This also confirms the stability of the control policy.

Convergence curves of weight estimate value W^i,s.

Because the V-SNAC structure adopted by our method reduces the number of neural networks, we have compared its computational time with the traditional AC structure [39]. Table II records the computational time required for a single step of control under the two network structures, denoted as “time per step.” The comparative analysis reveals that the V-SNAC framework achieves a reduction of approximately 31% in computation time per step, which demonstrate the efficiency of the V-SNAC structure and provides a possibility for faster decision-making in the context of the MPE game.

TABLE II Comparative Analysis of Computation Burden in V-SNAC and AC Networks

Remark 6:

The abovementioned two simulation scenarios represent two categories of typical cases. Under the assumption that Np≥Ne, the MPE game can be classified into the aforementioned combinations of multi-pursuer-multi-evader and multi-pursuer-single-evader, which can be solved in the same manner. Therefore, the simulation examples confirm the effectiveness of the designed off-policy RL Algorithm with dynamic target graph and V-SNAC structure. Furthermore, it also shows that the off-policy RL scheme is applicable to the nonlinear MPE games with constrained inputs.

SECTION V.

Conclusion

An approximate optimal control strategy based on reinforcement learning has been designed and applied to the multiagent PE game in this article. The relationships between agents are represented using graph models. The MPE game is constrained by actuator saturation and nonlinear system dynamics. Initially, using the proposed approximate HJI equation, we present an on-policy PI algorithm with convergence analysis. Then, to approximate the value functions, an off-policy RL method is introduced. This algorithm efficiently solves the approximate HJI equation and provides solutions under multiagent conditions. We utilize a network based on the V-SNAC structure to implement this off-policy RL method. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the proof of the network system's UUB is provided. Finally, we conduct simulations in two distinct scenarios: multiple-pursuer-one-evader and multiple-pursuer-multiple-evader. Comparative analyzes on cohesion and computational burden are employed to verify the effectiveness. In future research, attention can be focused on enhancing the collaboration among evaders, as well as addressing the problem of MPE in situations with limited state perception and communication.
